summary: Provides a framework for analyzing how SDP attributes behave when several media descriptions share a single transport address, as with BUNDLE. It also categorizes existing SDP attributes according to their multiplexing characteristics. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: When many streams share a single box, some labels still make sense and others clash. This document gives a method for sorting labels into those that can safely share and those that cannot.

questions: which sdp attributes work with multiplexing
how are sdp attributes categorized for bundle
what does mux category identical mean
what is the sdp transport mux category
subtitle: A way to sort SDP attributes by how they behave when many media streams share one transport flow.

tldr.problem: When several SDP media descriptions share one 5-tuple, attributes that were fine on separate m= lines can clash or become ambiguous. With close to 250 registered attributes and more coming, there was no procedure to judge them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines nine multiplexing categories (NORMAL, CAUTION, IDENTICAL, SUM, TRANSPORT, INHERIT, IDENTICAL-PER-PT, SPECIAL, TBD), assigns one to each existing attribute in long tables, and has IANA add a 'Mux Category' column to the SDP registries.
tldr.outcome: A designer or implementer can look up an attribute's category to know whether it can differ per media description, must be identical, or should not be multiplexed. New attributes are expected to say which category they belong to.

today: RFC 8859 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and it has not been obsoleted. Its categories are used by RFC 8858, which marks rtcp-mux-only as IDENTICAL.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SDP has attributes for single media descriptions (the m= lines) and for the whole session. Normally, different media types such as audio and video are separate RTP sessions on separate transport flows. RFC 8843 defines BUNDLE, which lets several media descriptions share one address and port, so one set of ICE candidates can serve all of them.

That raises a question: what does each attribute mean when its media description is multiplexed? This RFC provides a framework to analyze attributes for multiplexing, and then applies it to the attributes registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: People used to send each kind of mail in its own truck. Now several kinds share one truck, so we need to know which labels still work.

sections.title: The Problem with Shared Transport
sections.content:
Cutting the number of transport flows saves time and effort: setting up SRTP over ICE and DTLS is slow and complicated, and sharing helps conserve port bindings on NATs.

The catch is that some attribute combinations make sense on independent m= lines but not when those lines share a transport. The RFC's example is ice-ufrag: ICE allows each m= line its own value, but if the media are multiplexed over the same ICE component, the meaning of per-media values becomes muddled.

The text notes that close to 250 SDP attributes were registered with IANA when it was written, and that there was no clear procedure to decide whether they apply under transport multiplexing.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kids may each have their own password for a game, but if they share one computer account, the game cannot tell which password to use.

sections.title: The Nine Multiplexing Categories
sections.content:
Each attribute is assigned to a category. The categories are independent of any informal grouping of attributes, so the assignments are normative.

  • NORMAL: can be set independently on each media description and keeps its meaning. Examples are direction attributes and label.
  • CAUTION: not advisable to multiplex, since it may cause incorrect behavior. DCCP is the example, because it is connection oriented and does not allow multiple connections on the same 5-tuple.
  • IDENTICAL: the attribute and its values MUST be repeated across all multiplexed media descriptions. rtcp-mux is the example. RFC 8843 defines when such attributes can apply implicitly.
  • SUM: usable as normal, but software MUST apply the sum across the multiplexed descriptions. The example adds b=AS:64 and b=AS:256 into 256+64 kilobits per second.
  • TRANSPORT: may be set on several descriptions, but software MUST use the one from the m= line chosen to set up the transport. In a BUNDLE group, that is the first mid on the a=group:BUNDLE line.
  • INHERIT: attributes that wrap other attributes take on the category of what they wrap; the wrapped ones MUST be coherent.
  • IDENTICAL-PER-PT: payload-type-scoped attributes MUST be identical across descriptions for the same payload type, when repeated.
  • SPECIAL: the defining specification MUST be consulted. extmap is the example.
  • TBD: not analyzed under this framework, and SHOULD NOT be multiplexed.
sections.plainLanguage: Nine bins: some labels can differ freely, some must match everywhere, some add up, some follow whoever drives the truck, and a few are unknown so you should leave them alone.

sections.title: Analysis of Existing Attributes
sections.content:
Sections 5 to 13 apply the framework to attributes from the IANA registry, grouped under the RFC that defines each. Every table lists the attribute name, notes, level (S for session, M for media, B for both, SR for a single source) and its mux category. The long tables are reference material, so here are a few representative results.

  • rtcp-mux and rtcp-rsize are IDENTICAL, because they affect the entire RTP session.
  • ice-ufrag, ice-pwd, candidate, crypto and rtcp are TRANSPORT.
  • rtpmap, fmtp, ptime and rtcp-fb are IDENTICAL-PER-PT.
  • label and the sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly and inactive direction attributes are NORMAL.
  • extmap is SPECIAL, and the k= line is CAUTION.

Later sections handle attributes with several values, such as bwtype, rtcp-fb, group, ssrc-group, QoS tokens, content and payload formats. For example, group semantics such as group:FID and group:DUP are NORMAL, group:ANAT is CAUTION because ANAT is obsolete, and the ulpfec payload formats are CAUTION because of reuse of SSRCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the authors go through a very long list of labels and put each in a bin, with a short note on why.

sections.title: Capability Negotiation Under Multiplexing
sections.content:
Some attributes carry other attributes. a=cpar (RFC 3407) wraps a bandwidth line or an attribute and inherits its category: SUM for bandwidth, otherwise the category of the wrapped attribute. In the example, cpar wrapping rtcp-mux inherits IDENTICAL.

For SDP Capability Negotiation (RFC 5939), the offerer lists potential configurations with a=pcfg. To make it easy for the answerer to pick a consistent set across a BUNDLE group, every media description that has potential configurations MUST have at least one with the same configuration number (for example 1). The offerer MUST ensure that if the answerer picks number x in all of them, the result satisfies the multiplexing constraints. The answerer simply picks a number that appears in all of them.

For RFC 6871 media capabilities, the same payload type number in different descriptions must follow the BUNDLE rules and refer to the same codec configuration. Use of a=sescap is not recommended with multiplexed media, because it needs unique configuration numbers across the SDP, so valid combinations of latent configurations can only be found by attempting negotiation later.
sections.plainLanguage: When one label holds another label inside it, the inside label decides which bin it goes in. When offering choices, number the matching choices the same way so the other side can pick one easily.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA created a new 'Multiplexing Categories' subregistry with the nine categories, all referencing RFC 8859. Further entries need Standards Action (RFC 8126), meaning IESG review and a Standards Track RFC. A new category must also say how it applies to the SDP subregistries.

IANA also added a 'Mux Category' column to several subregistries of the 'Session Description Protocol (SDP) Parameters' registry, and the tables in Section 15.2 give the values. Entries that lack a value in this specification get TBD.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of labels gained a new column that shows each label's bin, and any entry nobody sorted is marked TBD.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The primary security considerations for RTP, including the way it is used here, are in RFC 3550 and RFC 3711.

When multiplexing attributes in the CAUTION category, implementations should be aware of the issues this specification describes.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules come from the older documents, and anyone using a 'careful' label should read the warning next to it.

items.label: Independent
items.desc: Set per media description; keeps its meaning.

items.label: Repeat everywhere
items.desc: Same value on all multiplexed media descriptions.

items.label: Add up
items.desc: Apply the sum, such as for bandwidth.

items.label: Use the transport one
items.desc: Use the value from the m= line that sets up the transport.

items.label: Follow the wrapped attribute
items.desc: Takes the category of what it encapsulates.

items.label: Same per payload type
items.desc: Identical for a given payload type across descriptions.

items.label: Read the defining spec
items.desc: Behavior is defined by the specification of the attribute.

data.title: Same configuration number in audio and video
data.code:
a=tcap:1 RTP/SAVPF
a=tcap:2 RTP/SAVP
a=group:BUNDLE audio video
m=audio
a=mid:audio
a=pcfg:1 t=1
a=pcfg:2
m=video
a=mid:video
a=pcfg:1 t=1
a=pcfg:2 t=2
